talk: A down round means raising money at a lower price than last time. It dilutes everyone more, and investors with anti-dilution protection get extra shares to make up for it. Founders usually pay for most of that protection.

terms.meaning: A round priced lower than the one before.
A term that gives earlier investors extra shares if a later round is cheaper.
The harshest version: earlier investors are repriced to the new, lower price.

questions.prompt: Last round, investors paid $2 a share. Now the club raises at $1.50 a share. By what percentage did the price fall?
questions.hint: Measure the drop against the old price.
whyNot: $1.50 / $2 = 75% is what's left of the price, not how much it fell.
$0.50 / $1.50 = about 33% divides by the new price. Measure the fall against where you started, $2.

questions.prompt: An earlier investor bought 1M shares at $2 with full ratchet protection. Repriced to $1.50, how many shares do they hold now?
questions.hint: Their money divided by the new price.
whyNot: $2M is the money they paid, not the shares.
1M x 1.5 = 1.5M multiplies by the new price instead of dividing the money by it.
Without protection they'd stay at 1M. Full ratchet reprices their whole $2M.

questions.prompt: Who pays for those extra shares?
options: Founders and other owners without protection
questions.hint: Who ends up with a smaller slice?
working: The extra shares go to the protected investor with no new money coming in.
Everyone without protection owns a smaller slice. That's usually the founders and staff.
whyNot: The new investor pays the new price and gets exactly what they paid for.
The protected investor is the one receiving the extra shares.
New shares always come out of someone's slice.

penalty.prompt: An earlier investor bought {shares} shares at {old} with full ratchet protection. The new round is priced at {now} a share. How many shares do they hold after repricing?
penalty.hint: Their money divided by the new price.

traps.why: Without protection they'd keep {shares}. Full ratchet reprices their whole investment.
Upside down. A lower price means more shares for the same money.

call.title: The down round
call.prompt: The club needs $3M and the only offer values it at $6M pre-money, half your last valuation. Earlier investors have full ratchet protection, which would hand them another 10% of the club. The money would add about 1,000 fans a match. Deep cuts instead would lose about 800.

options.label: Take it, ratchet and all
options.result: $6M + $3M = $9M post-money, so the new investor gets $3M / $9M = about 33%. The ratchet adds 10% more, all out of everyone without protection, you included.

options.label: Ask earlier investors to waive the ratchet for a 2% sweetener
options.result: Good call. Earlier investors often waive protection when the alternative is a club in trouble. Giving 2% to save 10% - 2% = 8% of the club is a good trade.

options.label: No raise, make deep cuts
options.result: Avoiding the round costs 800 fans a match: 800 x $18 = $14,400 every matchday.

takeaway: In a down round, protection for some investors is paid by everyone else. Negotiate it.
